title: Kashmir
wiki_lead:
Kashmir ( KASH-meer or  kash-MEER) is the northernmost geographical region of the Indian subcontinent. Until the mid-19th century, the term Kashmir denoted only the Kashmir Valley between the Great Himalayas and the Pir Panjal Range. The term has since also come to encompass a larger area that formerly comprised the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, and includes the Indian-administered territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, the Pakistani-administered territories of Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, and the Chinese-administered territories of Aksai Chin and the Trans-Karakoram Tract.
In the first millennium, the Kashmir region became an important centre of Buddhism. In the second half of the first millennium, the Karakotas ruled Kashmir, most notably Lalitaditya Muktapida; they were followed by the Loharas. Later still, in the ninth century, Kashmir Shaivism arose. In 1339, Shah Mir became the first Muslim ruler of Kashmir, inaugurating the Shah Miri dynasty dynasty, which ruled until 1568;  most notable was Zain Ul Abedin. Sufism flowered, especially through Nund Rishi.  Mughal rule began with Akbar,  who conquered Kashmir in 1586, and lasted until 1751, followed by the Afghan Durrani Empire, which ruled from 1751 until 1820. That year, the Sikhs, under Ranjit Singh, annexed Kashmir.  In 1846, after the Sikh defeat in the First Anglo-Sikh War, and upon the purchase of the region from the British under the Treaty of Amritsar, the Raja of Jammu, Gulab Singh, became the new ruler of Jammu and Kashmir. The rule of his descendants, under the paramountcy (or tutelage) of the British Crown, lasted until the Partition of India in 1947, when the former princely state of the British Indian Empire became a disputed territory, now administered by three countries: China, India, and Pakistan.

Mughal rule began with Akbar,  who conquered Kashmir in 1586, and lasted until 1751, followed by the Afghan Durrani Empire, which ruled from 1751 until 1820. The rule of his descendants, under the paramountcy (or tutelage) of the British Crown, lasted until the Partition of India in 1947, when the former princely state of the British Indian Empire became a disputed territory, now administered by three countries: China, India, and Pakistan.


Etymology
The word Kashmir is thought to have been derived from Sanskrit and was referred to as káśmīra. A popular local etymology of Kashmir is that it is land desiccated from water. An alternative etymology attributes the name to the Vedic sage Kashyapa, who is believed to have settled people in this land. Accordingly, Kashmir is derived from either kashyapa-mir (Kashyapa's Lake) or kashyapa-meru (Kashyapa's Mountain).
While early references to Kashmir can be found in Hindu texts such as Mahabharata and the puranas such as Matsya Purana, Vayu Purana, Padma Purana, Vishnu Purana, and Vishnudharmottara Purana, the earliest text which mentions the name Kashmir is the Ashtadhyayi by the Sanskrit grammarian Pāṇini in the 5th century BCE. Pāṇini calls the people of Kashmir Kashmirikas. 
The Ancient Greeks called the region Kasperia, which has been identified with Kaspapyros of Hecataeus of Miletus (apud Stephanus of Byzantium) and Kaspatyros of Herodotus (3.102, 4.44). Kashmir is also believed to be the country meant by Ptolemy's Kaspeiria.
Kashmir is mentioned as "Sharada Desha" (land of Sharada), in the 11th century Sanskrit poems by Bilhana. Sharada refers to the Hindu goddess Saraswati, and Kashmir has been the seat of Sharada Peeth, one of the historical centers of learning in the Indian subcontinent.
Kashmir is known as Kasheer in Kashmiri language. Buddhist scholar and traveller Huientsang called it kia-shi-milo, while some other Chinese accounts refer to Kashmir as ki-pin and ache-pin. Cashmere is an archaic spelling of Kashmir used in English.


Terminology
The Government of India and Indian sources refer to the territory under Pakistan control as "Pakistan-occupied Kashmir" ("POK"). The Government of Pakistan and Pakistani sources refer to the portion of Kashmir administered by India as "Indian-occupied Kashmir" ("IOK") or "Indian-held Kashmir" (IHK). The terms "Pakistan-administered Kashmir" and "India-administered Kashmir" are generally used by neutral sources for the parts of the Kashmir region controlled by each country.

grok_lead: Kashmir is a disputed Himalayan region in the Indian subcontinent, encompassing diverse mountainous terrain, high plateaus, and fertile valleys, strategically positioned between India, Pakistan, and China. The area, covering roughly 222,000 square kilometers, features notable natural landmarks such as the Kashmir Valley, Nanga Parbat peak, and the Indus River basin, contributing to its historical significance as a crossroads of trade and culture. Currently, the region is partitioned with India administering about 55% including the densely populated Kashmir Valley and Jammu areas with around 10 million residents, Pakistan controlling 35% via Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan with approximately 4.5 million people, and China holding 10% in Aksai Chin. This division stems from the 1947 partition of British India, when the Muslim-majority princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, under Hindu Maharaja Hari Singh, acceded to India after an invasion by Pakistani-backed Pashtun tribesmen prompted military assistance requests, igniting the first Indo-Pakistani war and resulting in a UN-mediated ceasefire along the Line of Control. The ensuing conflict, marked by further wars in 1965 and 1971, a 1999 Kargil incursion, and persistent militancy in Indian-administered areas, has caused tens of thousands of deaths, mass displacement, and economic stagnation, while UN resolutions advocating a plebiscite remain unimplemented due to disagreements over preconditions like troop withdrawals. In 2019, India abrogated Article 370 of its constitution, revoking Jammu and Kashmir's special autonomy, reorganizing it into two union territoriesâJammu and Kashmir and Ladakhâto promote direct governance and development, though this elicited accusations of demographic engineering and suppression from Pakistani and separatist perspectives. Despite the turmoil, Kashmir retains cultural prominence through its syncretic heritage, including Kashmiri Shaivism and Sufi traditions, and economic potential in tourism, horticulture, and hydropower, though security concerns and cross-border terrorismâlargely driven by Pakistan-backed militant groups âcontinue to hinder progress.
